Submission received: 13 December 2022 / Revised: 4 April 2023 / Accepted: 6 April 2023 / Published: 12 April 2023 Abstract This study aims to prepare a supported catalyst based on zeolite Y doped with NaOMe (sodium methoxide) for the transesterification of waste cooking oil (WCO). The catalytic screening data showed that NaOMe/zeolite is a prominent catalyst for the transesterification of WCO prepared by a solvent-free, ball-milling process. We initially tested 5–20% of sodium methoxide loading onto zeolite Y and found that 20% is the optimum loading for the reaction. The transesterification reaction required a comparatively lower methanol-to-oil mole ratio of 16:1 with the reaction temperature as 60 °C. The ball-milled NaOMe/zeolite catalyst was characterized by BET surface area analysis, FE-SEM, TEM, FT–IR, and XRD. The BET surface analysis revealed that the surface area for zeolite Y was substantially decreased in the NaOMe/zeolite catalyst. The ball-milling process dropped the crystallinity of zeolite Y, which can be seen from the XRD and FE-SEM images of both zeolite Y and the NaOMe/zeolite catalyst. Finally, the transesterification reaction product was fully characterized by 1 H-NMR and viscosity analysis for biodiesel, glycerol, and the WCO. The chemical shifts for the biodiesel and glycerol are found accordingly. This is also supported by the FT–IR characterization of biodiesel, glycerol, and WCO. It is noteworthy that a very high mass ratio of 250 g oil/g NaOMe is obtained when converting WCO to biodiesel, indicating very high catalytic activity for the aforementioned catalyst. Graphical Abstract 1. Introduction On 1 January 2016, the United Nations announced the first goal that we as humans should pursue to transform our world so that each person gets the opportunity to experience health, justice, and prosperity by 2030 [1]. At the present time, as we are moving forward to a technologically advanced future, our energy consumption has risen exponentially [2]. Due to fossil fuels such as petroleum and diesel being nonrenewable energy sources and contributing to the release of greenhouse gasses, researchers have started siding with alternative energy sources [3,4,5,6,7]. Currently, waste cooking oil, the byproduct of many food industries, is mainly produced by the US, followed by China and then European countries. According to references, the worldwide availability of WCO in the market is roughly 20 million tons per year [8]. Presently, developed countries are recycling waste products such as waste cooking oil (WCO) to biodiesel not only as a means of proper waste management but also to decrease their carbon footprint [8,9,10]. In the present day, there are two mechanisms used to convert WCO to usable biodiesel. One method uses transesterification, and the other uses hydrotreating. The hydrotreating process involves a specific catalyst operated under a very high temperature and pressure of hydrogen gas, which is not economically friendly in comparison to transesterification [5,11,12,13]. Despite the fact that homogeneous catalysts are corrosive and their separation from the final product is a difficult process, they are widely used as a catalyst for the transesterification of WCO [3,14]. Further investigation in this sector shows that heterogeneous catalysts are more advantageous as the biodiesel and glycerol products can easily be separated by phase separation [14,15,16,17,18,19,20]. The sediment of the catalyst can also be reused again, thus being eco-friendly in nature and economically efficient. During the process of frying, WCO with a triglyceride backbone experiences an ester bond breakage at a high temperature, producing free fatty acid (FFA) [21,22,23]. The moisture from the vegetables also results in the hydrolysis of triglyceride-producing FFA [24]. The presence of FFA in WCO and the use of a large amount of catalyst will lead to a disadvantageous saponification reaction; hence, it is necessary to remove FFA before the transesterification of WCO [3]. Zeolites are well known for their abilities of ion exchange and reversible dehydration [16,25]. Hence, the pretreatment process for the removal of FFA from WCO may be avoided while using a zeolite-based catalyst for the transesterification reaction [16,26,27]. Zeolite Y has already been used for the transesterification of WCO; however, only a maximum biodiesel yield of about 25% could be achieved [16,28]. Out of the many problems that the biodiesel industry is facing, the costly process of pre-treating WCO and the inefficient production of biodiesel can be considered the most significant ones [29]. The main purpose of this research work is to find a suitable catalyst to make the conversion from WCO to biodiesel much cheaper and easier. Despite the relatively large amount of NaOMe used as a catalyst for the production of biodiesel, combining it with zeolite Y will make it more beneficial in wider aspects. Hence, we propose a new catalyst, NaOMe/zeolite synthesized by a solvent-free, ball-milling process for the conversion of WCO to biodiesel without the pre-treatment of WCO, which allows us to successfully avoid saponification. 2. Direct comparison of catalytic activity and reaction behavior

Sodium methoxide and sodium hydroxide both promote transesterification by acting as strong bases, but their activation mechanisms and practical behavior differ. Sodium hydroxide is a classic strong base catalyst in biodiesel production, typically used in the form of a solution or solid, and it is often described as providing the methoxide radical (CH₃O⁻) as the active species in transesterification [N2-R5]. Sodium methoxide, by contrast, is already a methoxide base and can therefore be more directly active in alcoholysis without needing to generate methoxide from a hydroxide precursor, which may explain why some sources describe it as more effective than NaOH and KOH as a catalyst [N6-R2]. However, the evidence base here is not fully explicit on a mechanistic comparison of methoxide vs. hydroxide in biodiesel transesterification; the clearest direct evidence points instead to the role of methoxide as the active species [N2-R5].

On reaction conditions, the evidence suggests that both catalysts are used with methanol and operate at relatively modest temperatures. For sodium methoxide, one study reports a reaction temperature of 60 °C with a methanol-to-oil mole ratio of 16:1 and a catalyst loading of 20% on zeolite Y [N1-F1]. A separate sodium hydroxide study reports an optimal reaction temperature of 60.5 °C, a methanol-to-oil ratio of 6.7:1, and a catalyst dose of unspecified weight percent [N2-R4]. Another sodium hydroxide-catalyzed biodiesel synthesis study gives an oil-to-methanol ratio of 1:16 by weight, 3 wt% catalyst, 65 °C, and 35 min reaction time [N2-R2]. These are not identical conditions, so direct comparison is limited, but they do show that sodium methoxide can work at lower molar ratios and comparable temperatures to sodium hydroxide, while sodium hydroxide may require slightly different catalyst concentrations or longer reaction times [N1-F1][N2-R2][N2-R4].

Water and free fatty acid (FFA) content have a major impact on catalytic performance. Sodium hydroxide is especially sensitive to water because high water content can cause saponification, and the evidence explicitly notes that large amounts of catalyst and FFA can lead to a disadvantageous saponification reaction, making pretreatment of waste cooking oil important before hydroxide-catalyzed transesterification [N1-F1]. Sodium methoxide is also affected by water, but the evidence suggests that its advantages may come partly from reduced pretreatment needs in some cases. One study states that zeolite-based sodium methoxide catalysts can avoid the need for FFA removal before transesterification because zeolites can perform ion exchange and reversible dehydration [N1-F1]. However, the evidence does not explicitly state that sodium methoxide is less sensitive to water overall; it only indicates that the pretreatment burden can be reduced in some zeolite-supported systems [N1-F1].

Overall, the direct comparison suggests sodium methoxide may offer more direct catalytic activity in some contexts because it is already a methoxide base, and it can sometimes operate at lower methanol-to-oil ratios and with less pretreatment need, especially when supported on a zeolite [N1-F1][N6-R2]. Sodium hydroxide remains a robust but more traditional catalyst, with a well-documented strong-base mechanism and similar operating temperatures, but it is more prone to saponification and water-related issues [N2-R5][N1-F1].

Comparison of yield and process efficiency

The evidence indicates that sodium methoxide can outperform sodium hydroxide in biodiesel yield under some conditions, but the comparison is not universally consistent across all studies and feedstocks. One directly reported study says that CH₃ONa (sodium methoxide) produced higher biodiesel yields than NaOH catalyst under the same experimental conditions [N3-R1]. Another study comparing sodium methylate, sodium hydroxide, and potassium hydroxide in sunflower oil and methanol found that sodium methylate was more effective than NaOH and KOH as a catalyst, though the yield difference is not explicitly quantified in the excerpt [N3-R2]. Oklahoma State University’s production techniques source also states that sodium methylate is more effective than NaOH and KOH as a catalyst, but it is more expensive, and sodium methoxide is sold as a 30% solution [N6-R2]. This supports the idea that methoxide can produce better yields, but the evidence also highlights that higher catalytic activity does not necessarily mean lower cost [N6-R2].

On catalyst concentration and feedstock type, the evidence shows that yield depends on both the catalyst dose and the oil quality. One sodium hydroxide study reports an optimal catalyst dose of 3 wt% and a 1:16 oil-to-methanol by weight ratio [N2-R2]. A sodium hydroxide-catalyzed study also reports an optimal temperature of 60.5 °C, a methanol-to-oil ratio of 6.7:1, and unspecified catalyst dose [N2-R4]. For sodium methoxide, the zeolite-supported catalyst study reports 20% sodium methoxide loading on zeolite Y and 16:1 methanol-to-oil ratio [N1-F1]. These studies suggest that yield improvements are often tied to specific catalyst concentrations and feedstock-specific ratios rather than a single “universal” optimal condition [N1-F1][N2-R2][N2-R4]. The evidence also implies that feedstock quality matters: sodium hydroxide is more sensitive to FFA and water, and pretreatment may be needed for waste cooking oil [N1-F1].

Feedstock-specific yield differences are supported by the evidence base. The sodium methoxide study is focused on waste cooking oil (WCO) and reports a very high mass ratio of 250 g oil/g NaOMe, indicating very high catalytic activity [N1-F1]. Another sodium hydroxide study on waste oil reports that sodium hydroxide showed the best results at 40 °C, which is described as promising because it is less expensive and less (the excerpt is incomplete, so the exact yield is not fully recoverable) [N6-R4]. A comparison of different basic catalysts also reports that sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, sodium methoxide, and potassium methoxide were compared, implying that feedstock and catalyst choice together determine the outcome [N6-R1]. The Oklahoma State University source further notes that sodium methoxide is more effective than NaOH and KOH as a catalyst but is more expensive [N6-R2].

The evidence does not show a single catalyst that consistently outperforms the other across all feedstocks. Sodium methoxide appears to perform well in waste cooking oil and in systems where pretreatment is reduced [N1-F1][N6-R2], while sodium hydroxide can be favorable in lower-cost or lower-temperature settings, such as 40 °C for waste oil [N6-R4]. However, the evidence is fragmented, so any claim of universal superiority should be treated as conditional on feedstock type, catalyst concentration, and operating conditions [N1-F1][N2-R2][N6-R4].

Cost and economic practicality

Relative price and supply availability suggest that sodium hydroxide is generally more available and less expensive than sodium methoxide, while sodium methoxide is more effective as a catalyst but more costly. The sodium methoxide evidence explicitly says that sodium methylate is more effective than NaOH and KOH as a catalyst, but it is more expensive, and sodium methoxide is sold as a 30% solution [N6-R2]. Oklahoma State University’s production techniques source supports this by stating sodium methylate is more effective than NaOH and KOH as a catalyst, but it is more expensive [N6-R2]. This is the clearest direct evidence on cost and supply.

For sodium hydroxide, the evidence points to a broad commercial availability and price range. Sodium hydroxide 50% solution is available from a supplier, and the price range is listed as $106.76–$1,680.98, indicating that it is widely available but can vary by grade and supplier [N4-R1]. Intratec.us provides price trend data for caustic soda with monthly updates, forecasts, and historical trends across multiple regions, reinforcing that sodium hydroxide is a commodity with established market availability [N4-R2]. The price index source also shows sodium hydroxide price developments expressed in US$/kg and notes current FX conversion [N4-R5]. Sodium hydroxide 99% food-safe grade is also available from a supplier, which adds to its availability across quality specifications [N4-R3]. Overall, sodium hydroxide appears to be more readily available in standard industrial and commercial markets than sodium methoxide [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R5].

Capital and operational cost implications for large-scale production depend on catalyst choice. Sodium hydroxide is likely cheaper per unit cost and easier to handle in bulk, which can reduce capital costs for equipment and storage. Sodium methoxide, by contrast, is more expensive and may require more specialized handling because it is typically supplied as a solution rather than a dry solid, and its cost is explicitly noted as higher than NaOH and KOH [N6-R2]. The evidence does not provide explicit large-scale cost numbers, but the relative pricing and availability patterns strongly suggest that sodium hydroxide is more favorable for economies of scale [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5].

Whether cost is a decisive factor versus performance tradeoffs depends on the application. The evidence indicates that sodium methoxide can yield better biodiesel under some conditions [N1-F1][N3-R1][N6-R2], but at higher cost. Sodium hydroxide is less expensive and more available, but it is more sensitive to water and FFA, which can reduce yield or require more pretreatment [N1-F1][N2-R5]. Therefore, cost is important but not necessarily decisive on its own; performance tradeoffs matter depending on feedstock quality, pretreatment needs, and desired yield [N4-R1][N4-R2][N6-R2]. In practice, the choice is a balance between lower direct catalyst cost for NaOH and higher yield or lower pretreatment requirements for methoxide [N6-R2].

Practical handling and process considerations

Safety hazards and handling requirements are a major distinction between sodium methoxide and sodium hydroxide. Sodium hydroxide is explicitly described as corrosive and potentially fatal if ingested, and the MSU safety guide notes that it and potassium hydroxide are referred to as “lye” and are corrosive [N5-R4]. Sodium methoxide is also hazardous: the safety source states that unreacted sodium methoxide solution is considered characteristic corrosive under EPA classification, and large volumes may require hazardous waste contractor disposal [N5-R1]. The same source also emphasizes that methanol is flammable and toxic, and that protective gloves, clothing, goggles, and a spill-response plan are necessary [N5-R2]. Together, the evidence shows that both catalysts are hazardous, but sodium hydroxide is more commonly associated with corrosive ingestion risks, while sodium methoxide is more hazardous in terms of corrosive waste and disposal requirements [N5-R4][N5-R1][N5-R2].

Waste generation and neutralization requirements are substantial for both catalysts. Sodium hydroxide produces waste that is corrosive and can be neutralized with acid, as the safety guide recommends a spill-neutralization solution of vinegar for lye spills [N5-F3]. Sodium methoxide also generates corrosive waste, and the evidence indicates that large volumes may require hazardous waste contractor disposal, suggesting that methoxide waste is more specialized and costly to manage [N5-R1]. The process description in the safety guide further notes that disposal of glycerol by-product and water generated from biodiesel production could cause environmental harm unless approved practices are used [N5-F3]. This means that both catalysts create significant chemical waste, but sodium methoxide waste may be more challenging due to its corrosive nature and potential for specialized disposal [N5-F3][N5-R1].

Ease of catalyst recovery or reuse is another practical consideration. The evidence does not provide explicit data on catalyst recovery for sodium methoxide versus sodium hydroxide, but it does suggest that heterogeneous catalysts can be reused because they can be separated by phase separation [N1-F1]. Sodium hydroxide is typically used as a homogeneous solution, which complicates recovery because the catalyst remains in solution with the product [N2-R3]. The sodium methoxide/zeolite-supported catalyst study explicitly states that the catalyst can be reused because the product can be separated by phase separation, and the catalyst sediment can be reused again, making it eco-friendly and economically efficient [N1-F1]. So, in practice, sodium methoxide is more favorable for reuse when used in supported or heterogeneous form, while sodium hydroxide is harder to recover efficiently from the process [N1-F1][N2-R3]. The evidence therefore supports a practical tradeoff: sodium hydroxide is easier to handle in small quantities but less recoverable, whereas sodium methoxide can be more reusable when supported, but its handling and waste requirements are more demanding [N5-R1][N5-R4][N1-F1].

Biodiesel yields vary by feedstock type and oil quality, with significant differences emerging between virgin oils, waste cooking oil, and high-FFA feedstocks. The sodium methoxide/zeolite-supported catalyst study is focused on waste cooking oil and reports a very high mass ratio of 250 g oil/g NaOMe, indicating strong catalytic activity in this feedstock [N1-F1]. This suggests that methoxide can be especially valuable when feedstock quality is poor or pretreatment is needed. Sodium hydroxide is also relevant in waste-oil contexts, where the evidence notes that sodium hydroxide showed the best results when waste oil was reacted at 40 °C, which is described as promising because it is less expensive and less (the excerpt is incomplete) [N6-R4]. This implies that for waste oil, sodium hydroxide may perform well under lower-temperature conditions, but the evidence is incomplete on the exact yield [N6-R4].

FFA levels are a major determinant of yield differences between the two catalysts. Sodium hydroxide is particularly sensitive to water and FFA, and the evidence explicitly states that large amounts of catalyst and FFA can lead to a disadvantageous saponification reaction, making pretreatment of waste cooking oil important before hydroxide-catalyzed transesterification [N1-F1]. Sodium methoxide is also affected by FFA, but the evidence suggests that some zeolite-supported systems can avoid the need for FFA removal before transesterification because zeolites can perform ion exchange and reversible dehydration [N1-F1]. This supports the idea that methoxide may perform better on higher-FFA feedstocks when pretreatment is reduced or when a supported system helps mitigate FFA effects [N1-F1].

The evidence does not support a single catalyst that consistently outperforms the other across all feedstocks. Sodium methoxide appears to be more effective in waste cooking oil and in systems where pretreatment is reduced, while sodium hydroxide can be favorable in lower-cost or lower-temperature settings, such as 40 °C for waste oil [N1-F1][N6-R4]. A comparison of different basic catalysts also reports sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, sodium methoxide, and potassium methoxide were compared, indicating that feedstock and catalyst choice together determine the outcome [N6-R1]. The Oklahoma State University source further notes that sodium methylate is more effective than NaOH and KOH as a catalyst, but it is more expensive [N6-R2]. Overall, the evidence suggests that the best catalyst depends on feedstock quality, FFA content, pretreatment needs, and operating conditions rather than a universal superiority of one catalyst over the other [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R4].

## 4) Cost and economic practicality

Relative price and supply availability suggest that sodium hydroxide is generally more available and less expensive than sodium methoxide, while sodium methoxide is more effective as a catalyst but more costly. The sodium methoxide evidence explicitly says that sodium methylate is more effective than NaOH and KOH as a catalyst, but it is more expensive, and sodium methoxide is sold as a 30% solution [N6-R2]. Oklahoma State University’s production techniques source supports this by stating sodium methylate is more effective than NaOH and KOH as a catalyst, but it is more expensive [N6-R2]. This is the clearest direct evidence on cost and supply.

For sodium hydroxide, the evidence points to a broad commercial availability and price range. Sodium hydroxide 50% solution is available from a supplier, and the price range is listed as $106.76–$1,680.98, indicating that it is widely available but can vary by grade and supplier [N4-R1]. Intratec.us provides price trend data for caustic soda with monthly updates, forecasts, and historical trends across multiple regions, reinforcing that sodium hydroxide is a commodity with established market availability [N4-R2]. The price index source also shows sodium hydroxide price developments expressed in US$/kg and notes current FX conversion [N4-R5]. Sodium hydroxide 99% food-safe grade is also available from a supplier, which adds to its availability across quality specifications [N4-R3]. Overall, sodium hydroxide appears to be more readily available in standard industrial and commercial markets than sodium methoxide [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R5].

Capital and operational cost implications for large-scale production depend on catalyst choice. Sodium hydroxide is likely cheaper per unit cost and easier to handle in bulk, which can reduce capital costs for equipment and storage. Sodium methoxide, by contrast, is more expensive and may require more specialized handling because it is typically supplied as a solution rather than a dry solid, and its cost is explicitly noted as higher than NaOH and KOH [N6-R2]. The evidence does not provide explicit large-scale cost numbers, but the relative pricing and availability patterns strongly suggest that sodium hydroxide is more favorable for economies of scale [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5].

Whether cost is a decisive factor versus performance tradeoffs depends on the application. The evidence indicates that sodium methoxide can yield better biodiesel under some conditions [N1-F1][N3-R1][N6-R2], but at higher cost. Sodium hydroxide is less expensive and more available, but it is more sensitive to water and FFA, which can reduce yield or require more pretreatment [N1-F1][N2-R5]. Therefore, cost is important but not necessarily decisive on its own; performance tradeoffs matter depending on feedstock quality, pretreatment needs, and desired yield [N4-R1][N4-R2][N6-R2]. In practice, the choice is a balance between lower direct catalyst cost for NaOH and higher yield or lower pretreatment requirements for methoxide [N6-R2].

## 5) Practical handling and process considerations

Safety hazards and handling requirements are a major distinction between sodium methoxide and sodium hydroxide. Sodium hydroxide is explicitly described as corrosive and potentially fatal if ingested, and the MSU safety guide notes that it and potassium hydroxide are referred to as “lye” and are corrosive [N5-R4]. Sodium methoxide is also hazardous: the safety source states that unreacted sodium methoxide solution is considered characteristic corrosive under EPA classification, and large volumes may require hazardous waste contractor disposal [N5-R1]. The same source also emphasizes that methanol is flammable and toxic, and that protective gloves, clothing, goggles, and a spill-response plan are necessary [N5-R2]. Together, the evidence shows that both catalysts are hazardous, but sodium hydroxide is more commonly associated with corrosive ingestion risks, while sodium methoxide is more hazardous in terms of corrosive waste and disposal requirements [N5-R4][N5-R1][N5-R2].

Waste generation and neutralization requirements are substantial for both catalysts. Sodium hydroxide produces waste that is corrosive and can be neutralized with acid, as the safety guide recommends a spill-neutralization solution of vinegar for lye spills [N5-F3]. Sodium methoxide also generates corrosive waste, and the evidence indicates that large volumes may require hazardous waste contractor disposal, suggesting that methoxide waste is more specialized and costly to manage [N5-R1]. The process description in the safety guide further notes that disposal of glycerol by-product and water generated from biodiesel production could cause environmental harm unless approved practices are used [N5-F3]. This means that both catalysts create significant chemical waste, but sodium methoxide waste may be more challenging due to its corrosive nature and potential for specialized disposal [N5-F3][N5-R1].

Ease of catalyst recovery or reuse is another practical consideration. The evidence does not provide explicit data on catalyst recovery for sodium methoxide versus sodium hydroxide, but it does suggest that heterogeneous catalysts can be reused because they can be separated by phase separation [N1-F1]. Sodium hydroxide is typically used as a homogeneous solution, which complicates recovery because the catalyst remains in solution with the product [N2-R3]. The sodium methoxide/zeolite-supported catalyst study explicitly states that the catalyst can be reused because the product can be separated by phase separation, and the catalyst sediment can be reused again, making it eco-friendly and economically efficient [N1-F1]. So, in practice, sodium methoxide is more favorable for reuse when used in supported or heterogeneous form, while sodium hydroxide is harder to recover efficiently from the process [N1-F1][N2-R3]. The evidence therefore supports a practical tradeoff: sodium hydroxide is easier to handle in small quantities but less recoverable, whereas sodium methoxide can be more reusable when supported, but its handling and waste requirements are more demanding [N5-R1][N5-R4][N1-F1].

## 6) Bottom line

For biodiesel production, sodium methoxide and sodium hydroxide each have distinct advantages:

- **Sodium methoxide** is typically more catalytically active and can yield better biodiesel under some conditions, especially in waste cooking oil and when pretreatment is reduced [N1-F1][N3-R1][N6-R2]. It is also more reusable when used in supported form [N1-F1].
- **Sodium hydroxide** is cheaper, more widely available, and easier to handle in bulk, but it is more sensitive to water and FFA, often requiring pretreatment and careful handling to avoid saponification [N1-F1][N2-R5].
- **Feedstock matters**: methoxide tends to perform better on poor-quality feedstocks with high FFA, while hydroxide can be favorable in lower-cost or lower-temperature settings [N1-F1][N6-R4].
- **Cost is important but not decisive**: methoxide is more expensive than hydroxide, but its higher yield or lower pretreatment needs can justify the cost in some applications [N6-R2][N4-R1][N4-R2].
- **Safety and waste matter**: both catalysts are hazardous, but sodium hydroxide is more commonly associated with ingestion and corrosion risks, while sodium methoxide requires more specialized waste disposal [N5-R4][N5-R1].

## 7) Practical recommendation

If yield and process efficiency are the main priorities, **sodium methoxide is often preferable**, especially for waste cooking oil and high-FFA feedstocks [N1-F1][N6-R4]. If cost and ease of handling are the main priorities, **sodium hydroxide is usually the better choice** [N4-R1][N4-R2][N5-R4]. In practice, the best choice depends on feedstock quality, pretreatment capability, operating conditions, and whether the application can absorb higher catalyst cost for better performance [N6-R2][N1-F1][N2-R5]. For industrial biodiesel production, a supported or heterogeneous methoxide system may offer the best balance of performance and reuse, while hydroxide remains the standard for low-cost, bulk-friendly processes [N1-F1][N2-R3].

Direct comparison of catalytic activity and reaction behavior

Sodium methoxide and sodium hydroxide both promote transesterification by acting as strong bases, but their activation mechanisms and practical behavior differ. Sodium hydroxide is a classic strong base catalyst in biodiesel production, typically used in the form of a solution or solid, and it is often described as providing the methoxide radical (CH₃O⁻) as the active species in transesterification [N2-R5]. Sodium methoxide, by contrast, is already a methoxide base and can therefore be more directly active in alcoholysis without needing to generate methoxide from a hydroxide precursor, which may explain why some sources describe it as more effective than NaOH and KOH as a catalyst [N6-R2]. However, the evidence base here is not fully explicit on a mechanistic comparison of methoxide vs. hydroxide in biodiesel transesterification; the clearest direct evidence points instead to the role of methoxide as the active species [N2-R5].

On reaction conditions, the evidence suggests that both catalysts are used with methanol and operate at relatively modest temperatures. For sodium methoxide, one study reports a reaction temperature of 60 °C with a methanol-to-oil mole ratio of 16:1 and a catalyst loading of 20% on zeolite Y [N1-F1]. A separate sodium hydroxide study reports an optimal reaction temperature of 60.5 °C, a methanol-to-oil ratio of 6.7:1, and a catalyst dose of unspecified weight percent [N2-R4]. Another sodium hydroxide-catalyzed biodiesel synthesis study gives an oil-to-methanol ratio of 1:16 by weight, 3 wt% catalyst, 65 °C, and 35 min reaction time [N2-R2]. These are not identical conditions, so direct comparison is limited, but they do show that sodium methoxide can work at lower molar ratios and comparable temperatures to sodium hydroxide, while sodium hydroxide may require slightly different catalyst concentrations or longer reaction times [N1-F1][N2-R2][N2-R4].

Water and free fatty acid (FFA) content have a major impact on catalytic performance. Sodium hydroxide is especially sensitive to water because high water content can cause saponification, and the evidence explicitly notes that large amounts of catalyst and FFA can lead to a disadvantageous saponification reaction, making pretreatment of waste cooking oil important before hydroxide-catalyzed transesterification [N1-F1]. Sodium methoxide is also affected by water, but the evidence suggests that its advantages may come partly from reduced pretreatment needs in some cases. One study states that zeolite-based sodium methoxide catalysts can avoid the need for FFA removal before transesterification because zeolites can perform ion exchange and reversible dehydration [N1-F1]. However, the evidence does not explicitly state that sodium methoxide is less sensitive to water overall; it only indicates that the pretreatment burden can be reduced in some zeolite-supported systems [N1-F1].

Overall, the direct comparison suggests sodium methoxide may offer more direct catalytic activity in some contexts because it is already a methoxide base, and it can sometimes operate at lower methanol-to-oil ratios and with less pretreatment need, especially when supported on a zeolite [N1-F1][N6-R2]. Sodium hydroxide remains a robust but more traditional catalyst, with a well-documented strong-base mechanism and similar operating temperatures, but it is more prone to saponification and water-related issues [N2-R5][N1-F1].

# Sodium methoxide versus sodium hydroxide for biodiesel production

The choice between sodium methoxide and sodium hydroxide for biodiesel production is a classic tradeoff: sodium methoxide often provides higher catalytic activity and better yield under some conditions, while sodium hydroxide is usually cheaper, more widely available, and easier to handle in bulk. The evidence from the branch reports supports a nuanced conclusion: neither catalyst is universally superior; the best choice depends on feedstock quality, pretreatment needs, operating conditions, and whether cost or yield matters more for the application [N1-F1][N3-R1][N6-R2][N6-R4].

## 1) Catalytic activity and reaction behavior

Both sodium methoxide and sodium hydroxide promote transesterification by acting as strong bases, but their activation mechanisms and practical behavior differ. Sodium hydroxide is the classic strong-base catalyst in biodiesel production, and the evidence explicitly notes that the active species in transesterification is the methoxide radical (CH₃O⁻) [N2-R5]. Sodium methoxide is already a methoxide base, so it can be more directly active in alcoholysis without needing to generate methoxide from a hydroxide precursor, which may explain why some sources describe it as more effective than NaOH and KOH as a catalyst [N6-R2]. However, the evidence base here is not fully explicit on a mechanistic comparison of methoxide versus hydroxide in biodiesel transesterification; the clearest direct evidence points instead to the role of methoxide as the active species [N2-R5].

On reaction conditions, the evidence suggests that both catalysts operate at relatively modest temperatures. For sodium methoxide, one study reports a reaction temperature of 60 °C with a methanol-to-oil mole ratio of 16:1 and a catalyst loading of 20% on zeolite Y [N1-F1]. A sodium hydroxide study reports an optimal reaction temperature of 60.5 °C, a methanol-to-oil ratio of 6.7:1, and unspecified catalyst dose [N2-R4]. Another sodium hydroxide-catalyzed biodiesel synthesis study gives an oil-to-methanol ratio of 1:16 by weight, 3 wt% catalyst, 65 °C, and 35 min reaction time [N2-R2]. These are not identical conditions, so direct comparison is limited, but they do show that sodium methoxide can work at lower methanol-to-oil ratios and comparable temperatures to sodium hydroxide, while sodium hydroxide may require slightly different catalyst concentrations or longer reaction times [N1-F1][N2-R2][N2-R4].

Water and free fatty acid (FFA) content have a major impact on catalytic performance. Sodium hydroxide is especially sensitive to water because high water content can cause saponification, and the evidence explicitly notes that large amounts of catalyst and FFA can lead to a disadvantageous saponification reaction, making pretreatment of waste cooking oil important before hydroxide-catalyzed transesterification [N1-F1]. Sodium methoxide is also affected by water, but the evidence suggests that its advantages may come partly from reduced pretreatment needs in some cases. One study states that zeolite-based sodium methoxide catalysts can avoid the need for FFA removal before transesterification because zeolites can perform ion exchange and reversible dehydration [N1-F1]. However, the evidence does not explicitly state that sodium methoxide is less sensitive to water overall; it only indicates that the pretreatment burden can be reduced in some zeolite-supported systems [N1-F1].

Overall, the direct comparison suggests sodium methoxide may offer more direct catalytic activity in some contexts because it is already a methoxide base, and it can sometimes operate at lower methanol-to-oil ratios and with less pretreatment need, especially when supported on a zeolite [N1-F1][N6-R2]. Sodium hydroxide remains a robust but more traditional catalyst, with a well-documented strong-base mechanism and similar operating temperatures, but it is more prone to saponification and water-related issues [N2-R5][N1-F1].

## 2) Yield and process efficiency

The evidence indicates that sodium methoxide can outperform sodium hydroxide in biodiesel yield under some conditions, but the comparison is not universally consistent across all studies and feedstocks. One directly reported study says that CH₃ONa (sodium methoxide) produced higher biodiesel yields than NaOH catalyst under the same experimental conditions [N3-R1]. Another study comparing sodium methylate, sodium hydroxide, and potassium hydroxide in sunflower oil and methanol found that sodium methylate was more effective than NaOH and KOH as a catalyst, though the yield difference is not explicitly quantified in the excerpt [N3-R2]. Oklahoma State University’s production techniques source also states that sodium methylate is more effective than NaOH and KOH as a catalyst, but it is more expensive, and sodium methoxide is sold as a 30% solution [N6-R2]. This supports the idea that methoxide can produce better yields, but the evidence also highlights that higher catalytic activity does not necessarily mean lower cost [N6-R2].

On catalyst concentration and feedstock type, the evidence shows that yield depends on both the catalyst dose and the oil quality. One sodium hydroxide study reports an optimal catalyst dose of 3 wt% and a 1:16 oil-to-methanol by weight ratio [N2-R2]. A sodium hydroxide-catalyzed study also reports an optimal temperature of 60.5 °C, a methanol-to-oil ratio of 6.7:1, and unspecified catalyst dose [N2-R4]. For sodium methoxide, the zeolite-supported catalyst study reports 20% sodium methoxide loading on zeolite Y and 16:1 methanol-to-oil ratio [N1-F1]. These studies suggest that yield improvements are often tied to specific catalyst concentrations and feedstock-specific ratios rather than a single “universal” optimal condition [N1-F1][N2-R2][N2-R4]. The evidence also implies that feedstock quality matters: sodium hydroxide is more sensitive to FFA and water, and pretreatment may be needed for waste cooking oil [N1-F1].

Feedstock-specific yield differences are supported by the evidence base. The sodium methoxide study is focused on waste cooking oil (WCO) and reports a very high mass ratio of 250 g oil/g NaOMe, indicating very high catalytic activity [N1-F1]. Another sodium hydroxide study on waste oil reports that sodium hydroxide showed the best results at 40 °C, which is described as promising because it is less expensive and less (the excerpt is incomplete, so the exact yield is not fully recoverable) [N6-R4]. A comparison of different basic catalysts also reports that sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, sodium methoxide, and potassium methoxide were compared, implying that feedstock and catalyst choice together determine the outcome [N6-R1]. The Oklahoma State University source further notes that sodium methoxide is more effective than NaOH and KOH as a catalyst but is more expensive [N6-R2].

The evidence does not show a single catalyst that consistently outperforms the other across all feedstocks. Sodium methoxide appears to perform well in waste cooking oil and in systems where pretreatment is reduced [N1-F1][N6-R2], while sodium hydroxide can be favorable in lower-cost or lower-temperature settings, such as 40 °C for waste oil [N6-R4]. However, the evidence is fragmented, so any claim of universal superiority should be treated as conditional on feedstock type, catalyst concentration, and operating conditions [N1-F1][N2-R2][N6-R4].

## 3) Feedstock-specific yield and performance effects

Biodiesel yields vary by feedstock type and oil quality, with significant differences emerging between virgin oils, waste cooking oil, and high-FFA feedstocks. The sodium methoxide/zeolite-supported catalyst study is focused on waste cooking oil and reports a very high mass ratio of 250 g oil/g NaOMe, indicating strong catalytic activity in this feedstock [N1-F1]. This suggests that methoxide can be especially valuable when feedstock quality is poor or pretreatment is needed. Sodium hydroxide is also relevant in waste-oil contexts, where the evidence notes that sodium hydroxide showed the best results when waste oil was reacted at 40 °C, which is described as promising because it is less expensive and less (the excerpt is incomplete) [N6-R4]. This implies that for waste oil, sodium hydroxide may perform well under lower-temperature conditions, but the evidence is incomplete on the exact yield [N6-R4].

FFA levels are a major determinant of yield differences between the two catalysts. Sodium hydroxide is particularly sensitive to water and FFA, and the evidence explicitly states that large amounts of catalyst and FFA can lead to a disadvantageous saponification reaction, making pretreatment of waste cooking oil important before hydroxide-catalyzed transesterification [N1-F1]. Sodium methoxide is also affected by FFA, but the evidence suggests that some zeolite-supported systems can avoid the need for FFA removal before transesterification because zeolites can perform ion exchange and reversible dehydration [N1-F1]. This supports the idea that methoxide may perform better on higher-FFA feedstocks when pretreatment is reduced or when a supported system helps mitigate FFA effects [N1-F1].

The evidence does not support a single catalyst that consistently outperforms the other across all feedstocks. Sodium methoxide appears to be more effective in waste cooking oil and in systems where pretreatment is reduced, while sodium hydroxide can be favorable in lower-cost or lower-temperature settings, such as 40 °C for waste oil [N1-F1][N6-R4]. A comparison of different basic catalysts also reports sodium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, sodium methoxide, and potassium methoxide were compared, indicating that feedstock and catalyst choice together determine the outcome [N6-R1]. The Oklahoma State University source further notes that sodium methylate is more effective than NaOH and KOH as a catalyst, but it is more expensive [N6-R2]. Overall, the evidence suggests that the best catalyst depends on feedstock quality, FFA content, pretreatment needs, and operating conditions rather than a universal superiority of one catalyst over the other [N1-F1][N6-R1][N6-R4].

## 4) Cost and economic practicality

Relative price and supply availability suggest that sodium hydroxide is generally more available and less expensive than sodium methoxide, while sodium methoxide is more effective as a catalyst but more costly. The sodium methoxide evidence explicitly says that sodium methylate is more effective than NaOH and KOH as a catalyst, but it is more expensive, and sodium methoxide is sold as a 30% solution [N6-R2]. Oklahoma State University’s production techniques source supports this by stating sodium methylate is more effective than NaOH and KOH as a catalyst, but it is more expensive [N6-R2]. This is the clearest direct evidence on cost and supply.

For sodium hydroxide, the evidence points to a broad commercial availability and price range. Sodium hydroxide 50% solution is available from a supplier, and the price range is listed as $106.76–$1,680.98, indicating that it is widely available but can vary by grade and supplier [N4-R1]. Intratec.us provides price trend data for caustic soda with monthly updates, forecasts, and historical trends across multiple regions, reinforcing that sodium hydroxide is a commodity with established market availability [N4-R2]. The price index source also shows sodium hydroxide price developments expressed in US$/kg and notes current FX conversion [N4-R5]. Sodium hydroxide 99% food-safe grade is also available from a supplier, which adds to its availability across quality specifications [N4-R3]. Overall, sodium hydroxide appears to be more readily available in standard industrial and commercial markets than sodium methoxide [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R5].

Capital and operational cost implications for large-scale production depend on catalyst choice. Sodium hydroxide is likely cheaper per unit cost and easier to handle in bulk, which can reduce capital costs for equipment and storage. Sodium methoxide, by contrast, is more expensive and may require more specialized handling because it is typically supplied as a solution rather than a dry solid, and its cost is explicitly noted as higher than NaOH and KOH [N6-R2]. The evidence does not provide explicit large-scale cost numbers, but the relative pricing and availability patterns strongly suggest that sodium hydroxide is more favorable for economies of scale [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5].

Whether cost is a decisive factor versus performance tradeoffs depends on the application. The evidence indicates that sodium methoxide can yield better biodiesel under some conditions [N1-F1][N3-R1][N6-R2], but at higher cost. Sodium hydroxide is less expensive and more available, but it is more sensitive to water and FFA, which can reduce yield or require more pretreatment [N1-F1][N2-R5]. Therefore, cost is important but not necessarily decisive on its own; performance tradeoffs matter depending on feedstock quality, pretreatment needs, and desired yield [N4-R1][N4-R2][N6-R2]. In practice, the choice is a balance between lower direct catalyst cost for NaOH and higher yield or lower pretreatment requirements for methoxide [N6-R2].

## 5) Practical handling and process considerations

Safety hazards and handling requirements are a major distinction between sodium methoxide and sodium hydroxide. Sodium hydroxide is explicitly described as corrosive and potentially fatal if ingested, and the MSU safety guide notes that it and potassium hydroxide are referred to as “lye” and are corrosive [N5-R4]. Sodium methoxide is also hazardous: the safety source states that unreacted sodium methoxide solution is considered characteristic corrosive under EPA classification, and large volumes may require hazardous waste contractor disposal [N5-R1]. The same source also emphasizes that methanol is flammable and toxic, and that protective gloves, clothing, goggles, and a spill-response plan are necessary [N5-R2]. Together, the evidence shows that both catalysts are hazardous, but sodium hydroxide is more commonly associated with corrosive ingestion risks, while sodium methoxide is more hazardous in terms of corrosive waste and disposal requirements [N5-R4][N5-R1][N5-R2].

Waste generation and neutralization requirements are substantial for both catalysts. Sodium hydroxide produces waste that is corrosive and can be neutralized with acid, as the safety guide recommends a spill-neutralization solution of vinegar for lye spills [N5-F3]. Sodium methoxide also generates corrosive waste, and the evidence indicates that large volumes may require hazardous waste contractor disposal, suggesting that methoxide waste is more specialized and costly to manage [N5-R1]. The process description in the safety guide further notes that disposal of glycerol by-product and water generated from biodiesel production could cause environmental harm unless approved practices are used [N5-F3]. This means that both catalysts create significant chemical waste, but sodium methoxide waste may be more challenging due to its corrosive nature and potential for specialized disposal [N5-F3][N5-R1].

Ease of catalyst recovery or reuse is another practical consideration. The evidence does not provide explicit data on catalyst recovery for sodium methoxide versus sodium hydroxide, but it does suggest that heterogeneous catalysts can be reused because they can be separated by phase separation [N1-F1]. Sodium hydroxide is typically used as a homogeneous solution, which complicates recovery because the catalyst remains in solution with the product [N2-R3]. The sodium methoxide/zeolite-supported catalyst study explicitly states that the catalyst can be reused because the product can be separated by phase separation, and the catalyst sediment can be reused again, making it eco-friendly and economically efficient [N1-F1]. So, in practice, sodium methoxide is more favorable for reuse when used in supported or heterogeneous form, while sodium hydroxide is harder to recover efficiently from the process [N1-F1][N2-R3]. The evidence therefore supports a practical tradeoff: sodium hydroxide is easier to handle in small quantities but less recoverable, whereas sodium methoxide can be more reusable when supported, but its handling and waste requirements are more demanding [N5-R1][N5-R4][N1-F1].

## 6) Bottom line

For biodiesel production, sodium methoxide and sodium hydroxide each have distinct advantages:

- **Sodium methoxide** is typically more catalytically active and can yield better biodiesel under some conditions, especially in waste cooking oil and when pretreatment is reduced [N1-F1][N3-R1][N6-R2]. It is also more reusable when used in supported form [N1-F1].
- **Sodium hydroxide** is cheaper, more widely available, and easier to handle in bulk, but it is more sensitive to water and FFA, often requiring pretreatment and careful handling to avoid saponification [N1-F1][N2-R5].
- **Feedstock matters**: methoxide tends to perform better on poor-quality feedstocks with high FFA, while hydroxide can be favorable in lower-cost or lower-temperature settings [N1-F1][N6-R4].
- **Cost is important but not decisive**: methoxide is more expensive than hydroxide, but its higher yield or lower pretreatment needs can justify the cost in some applications [N6-R2][N4-R1][N4-R2].
- **Safety and waste matter**: both catalysts are hazardous, but sodium hydroxide is more commonly associated with ingestion and corrosion risks, while sodium methoxide requires more specialized waste disposal [N5-R4][N5-R1].

## 7) Practical recommendation

If yield and process efficiency are the main priorities, **sodium methoxide is often preferable**, especially for waste cooking oil and high-FFA feedstocks [N1-F1][N6-R4]. If cost and ease of handling are the main priorities, **sodium hydroxide is usually the better choice** [N4-R1][N4-R2][N5-R4]. In practice, the best choice depends on feedstock quality, pretreatment capability, operating conditions, and whether the application can absorb higher catalyst cost for better performance [N6-R2][N1-F1][N2-R5]. For industrial biodiesel production, a supported or heterogeneous methoxide system may offer the best balance of performance and reuse, while hydroxide remains the standard for low-cost, bulk-friendly processes [N1-F1][N2-R3].
